title: One extra argument
description:
Most standard algorithms accept an **execution policy** as their first argument. With `std::execution::par` the library splits the work across your processor's cores.

Write two functions, each a single parallel algorithm call:

- `long long sumOfSquares(const std::vector<int>& values)`: use `std::transform_reduce` with `std::execution::par`. It takes the range, a starting value (`0LL`), how to combine two results (`std::plus{}`), and how to transform each element (a lambda that squares it as a `long long`).
- `std::size_t countMultiples(const std::vector<int>& values, int divisor)`: use `std::count_if` with `std::execution::par`.

The lambdas must not touch anything shared: each one works only on its own argument and returns a result. That is what makes them safe to run in parallel.
